prompt: `toylm next "the coffee is"` printed five words with percentages. What were those percentages?
hint: Read the header of the table.

choices.text: The share of times each word followed `coffee is` in its file
choices.why: Right. A trigram model turns the counts of what followed a pair of words into percentages.

choices.text: How sure the model is that the coffee is hot
choices.why: It knows nothing about any coffee. It knows which words followed `coffee is` in its file.

choices.text: The share of the café's customers who would describe their coffee with each of those words
choices.why: There are no customers behind the numbers, only a file of 761 words.

choices.text: A ranking of answers to the question
choices.why: No question was asked. The command gave the model a piece of text and asked what comes next.

prompt: After `the coffee is`, the word `sweet` got no line at all. Why?
hint: Think about where every percentage came from.

choices.text: `sweet` is not one of the words in the model's vocabulary at all
choices.why: It is: the file says `the cake is sweet` three times. It is missing from this table because of where it appeared.

choices.text: The display hides every word scoring below 3%
choices.why: `--show` limits how many lines print, and it says how many it left out. Here nothing was left out.

choices.text: Sweet coffee is unusual in cafés
choices.why: The model has no idea what is usual for coffee. It has counts from one file.

choices.text: The file never has `sweet` after `coffee is`, only after `cake is`
choices.why: Yes. A word it never saw in that place gets nothing, even though `sweet` is in its vocabulary (`the cake is sweet`).

prompt: Which of these does a large language model do that `toylm` also does?
hint: The table compares the two on three rows. What did they share?

choices.text: It looks at the last two words only
choices.why: That is `toylm`'s window. A large model looks at a very long stretch of text, lesson 4.

choices.text: It keeps a table of how often each pair of words occurred in what it read
choices.why: A large model has learnt weights, not a table of counts.

choices.text: It scores every next piece
choices.why: Yes. Both output the same thing; they differ in how far back they look, what a piece is and where the scores come from.

choices.text: It splits the text it reads into whole words
choices.why: A large model splits text into tokens, which are pieces of words, lesson 3.

prompt: Somebody says the model "looked up" that the café opens at seven. What is wrong with the phrase?
hint: What did `toylm next` actually print for `the café opens at`?

choices.text: Nothing; it found the line in its file and returned it
choices.why: It did not return a line. It returned scores for the next word: `seven` 75%, `eight` 25%.

choices.text: It scored next words, and `eight` got a quarter
choices.why: Right. There is no lookup and no single stored answer; there is a distribution, and a quarter of it says `eight`.

choices.text: The model guessed at random, so seven was luck
choices.why: Not at random: `seven` had three times the score of `eight`, because it followed `opens at` three times as often.

choices.text: Models search the internet for a café's opening hours before they answer a question about them
choices.why: `toylm` has no network and no search. It has counts from 761 words.

prompt: `toylm` is a ___ model: it predicts the next word from counts of what followed each pair of words.
hint: The prefix means three: two words of context and the one predicted.

prompt: What does generation do after the model has scored the next word?
hint: Look at the loop in the figure.

choices.text: It picks one word, adds it to the text, and scores again
choices.why: Yes. Generation is that step in a loop.

choices.text: It writes the rest of the sentence from those scores
choices.why: The scores are only for the very next word. The rest needs the loop.

choices.text: It checks the word against a store of facts
choices.why: There is no such check in the loop. That is why a fluent sentence can be false.

choices.text: It asks the user which word to keep
choices.why: Nobody is asked. A rule picks, such as the highest score or a weighted draw.

prompt: `toylm generate "the cat sat on the" --temperature 0` wrote `chair by the window.` though the file says `the cat sat on the mat`. Why?
hint: Read the context line of `toylm next`.

choices.text: Temperature 0 picks the next word at random
choices.why: Temperature 0 picks the highest score every time, which here is `chair`.

choices.text: The model prefers to write the longer sentences
choices.why: It has no preference about length. It scored `chair` highest after `on the`.

choices.text: The file is wrong about where the cat sat
choices.why: The file says both things. The model could only see the part that mentions neither cat.

choices.text: `sat` is out of its two-word window
choices.why: Right. It sees only `on the`, where `chair` (3) beats `mat` (2).

prompt: `toylm generate "the café opens at" --temperature 0` printed `prompt 4 tokens, output 2 tokens`. How many tokens went in and came out together?
Five draws from `the coffee is` gave `hot` three times. What explains the other two?
hint: How does the command pick a word when temperature is not 0?

choices.text: The model was trained again between the draws
choices.why: Nothing changed in the model. Each draw used a different random seed.

choices.text: They came from a bug in the sampling code
choices.why: They are what weighted drawing is expected to produce.

choices.text: Words are drawn in proportion to their scores
choices.why: Yes. `hot` has 59.3%, so it should win about six draws in ten, and the rest go to the others.

choices.text: Draws ignore the scores and pick any word in the vocabulary with the same chance
choices.why: If they did, `bitter` would be as common as `hot`.

prompt: `the coffee is cold and the cat wakes.` came out of `toylm`. Which statement about it is true?
hint: Check the sentence against the file, pair by pair and as a whole.

choices.text: It is in the file, since the model repeats what it saw
choices.why: It repeats pairs. The sentence as a whole is new.

choices.text: Each pair of words is in the file; the sentence is not
choices.why: Right. Fluent text built from familiar pieces, with nothing behind it, which is how lesson 5 begins.

choices.text: It is ungrammatical, which is how you can tell
choices.why: It is perfectly grammatical. That is what makes this kind of error hard to spot.

choices.text: It shows the model worked out that cold coffee wakes the cat
choices.why: No reasoning took place. Each word followed the two words before it somewhere in the file.

prompt: `toylm` printed `finish: end`. What does that say?
hint: There are two reasons generation stops.

choices.text: The model picked the token that means the text is over, and the loop ended
choices.why: Yes. The other reason is a limit somebody set, lesson 15.

choices.text: It ran out of words
choices.why: Vocabulary has nothing to do with stopping.

choices.text: The output reached the maximum number of tokens allowed
choices.why: That reason is printed as `length`, not `end`.

choices.text: An error interrupted the loop
choices.why: Nothing failed. `end` is the normal way for a short answer to finish.

prompt: Why does a chat assistant answer a question instead of continuing it with another question?
hint: Was the mechanism changed, or what the model finds likely?

choices.text: A second program detects questions and writes the answers to them
choices.why: There is no second program writing answers. The same model writes the assistant's turn.

choices.text: Chat models predict whole sentences
choices.why: They still predict one token at a time.

choices.text: The question is removed before the model sees it
choices.why: The question is exactly what the model is given.

choices.text: Training made answering likely
choices.why: Right. The loop is the same; training changed what counts as likely after a question.

prompt: In this course, how can you tell a real capture from a reply written as an illustration?
hint: Look at what is in front of the first line.

choices.text: Illustrations are in English and captures are in Portuguese
choices.why: Both are in English inside the fence; the prompt is what tells them apart.

choices.text: Captures are shorter
choices.why: Length says nothing about where text came from.

choices.text: You cannot, so treat everything as an illustration
choices.why: There is a way: the prompt marks a capture, and an illustration is labelled as one.

choices.text: A capture starts with a prompt
choices.why: Yes. An illustration has no prompt, and the sentence before it says the course wrote it.

prompt: Which of these in the workbench are real software doing a real job? Choose all that apply.
hint: One tool's input is replayed from files the lessons write.

choices.text: `tok`, the tokenizer
choices.why: Yes: the o200k_base and cl100k_base encodings, the same ones production code uses.

choices.text: `toylm`, as a language model
choices.why: Yes. It is small, and it is a real language model built from real counts.

choices.text: The model's turns that `agent` reads
choices.why: Those are written by the lessons and played back. The loop around them is real; the turns are not a model's.

choices.text: `validate`, the JSON Schema check
choices.why: Yes: the `jsonschema` library.

prompt: You run a prompt from this course on a real model and get a different reply from the illustration. What does that mean?
hint: What did this section promise about illustrations?

choices.text: The model is broken and you should report it
choices.why: A different wording is expected, not a fault.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: replies vary between models and between two runs of one prompt
choices.why: Right. Lesson 13 explains the variation between two runs of the same prompt.

choices.text: The illustration was a capture that changed
choices.why: Illustrations are written by the course and say so. They were never captures.

choices.text: You have to run it again and again until the reply matches the one in the course
choices.why: No reply is guaranteed to match. Judge it against what you asked for.

prompt: Put one round of generation in order.
hint: It starts with the text that already exists.
items: Take the text written so far
Give every possible next word a score
Pick one word from the scores
Add that word to the end of the text

prompt: Match each part of `toylm` to the large language model's version of it.
hint: The table in the first section.

pairs.right: a window of up to hundreds of thousands of tokens

prompt: A model says, fluently, that a café you never mentioned opens at seven. What does this lesson say you can conclude?
hint: What is the model's output, underneath?

choices.text: It found the café's hours in its training data
choices.why: It may have; it may also have produced a typical opening time. The output alone does not say which.

choices.text: The confident wording means it checked the hours before it replied
choices.why: The wording is generated by the same loop as the hour. Nothing checked anything.

choices.text: The answer is wrong, since models cannot know facts
choices.why: Likely text is often true. The point is that you cannot tell which from the fluency.

choices.text: Seven was likely, which is not the same as true
choices.why: Right. A likely continuation and a fact coincide often, and not always.
